messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 35-year-old tutor who, until seven months ago, found deep satisfaction in her work and her stable relationship with her partner, Marcus. That life came to an abrupt halt on a Tuesday evening in March. She was home alone with her three-year-old son, who was asleep in his bedroom, when she answered a knock at the door, assuming it was a package delivery. The man forced his way inside. The details of the assault remain a chaotic blur of sensations, but what she remembers most clearly is the sound of her son waking up and beginning to cry from his room. His frightened wails formed a soundtrack to her own terror, a sound she was powerless to respond to, cementing a feeling of profound helplessness that has lingered ever since.

In the months that followed, the memory of that night has taken on a peculiar quality. When she tries to grasp it, it feels distant and unreal, like a disturbing film she once saw. She has come to think of the woman in that memory as a different person, someone she observes with a detached pity. Yet, this detachment offers no protection. When a memory fragment is triggered, the raw, physical terror of the event returns with full force. She has never been able to narrate what happened, not to the police and not to Marcus. The words simply will not form a coherent sequence; the experience lives in her body as a jumble of sounds, pressures, and the metallic taste of fear, but not as a story she can tell.

Her world has progressively shrunk as she tries to navigate a landscape mined with triggers. The most potent is the sound of a child crying. During a tutoring session at a client’s house two months ago, the family’s newborn began to wail in an adjacent room. Amina felt a wave of nausea so intense she thought she would be sick on the spot. Her heart hammered against her ribs, and the student’s living room momentarily dissolved, replaced by the image of her own son’s bedroom door. She abruptly ended the session, claiming a sudden migraine, and has since stopped taking on clients with young children, a decision that has significantly impacted her income. Any feeling of uncertainty, from a delayed text message from Marcus to a change in a lesson plan, can send a jolt of panic through her, a faint echo of the terrifying unknowing of the assault itself.

Amina’s days are now governed by a quiet, exhausting vigilance. She spends hours replaying the event in her mind, a litany of "if onlys." If only she hadn’t opened the door. If only she had fought harder. She is certain that the fault, somehow, was hers. This self-blame has become a constant companion, convincing her that she is fundamentally tainted. She has come to believe that she has been permanently changed for the worse, that the capable, joyful woman she once was is gone forever. This conviction makes her shy away from anything that might bring pleasure. When Marcus recently tried to book a surprise weekend away, she felt a surge of panic, not joy. The prospect of happiness felt like a trap, something she no longer deserved and could not sustain. She has learned to see even the slightest upset—a burnt piece of toast, a misplaced set of keys—as proof of her own fragility, confirmation of her deeply held belief that she can no longer cope with life.

She sought therapy after Marcus sat her down last week, his face etched with worry. He told her he felt a growing distance between them, that her refusal to talk about "that night" or engage with their life together was making him feel helpless. It was the fear of losing him, on top of everything else she felt she had lost, that finally propelled her to make an appointment. She confessed in her first session that her greatest fear is that thinking or talking about the event will cause her to shatter completely, that the protective wall of detachment will crumble and leave her with nothing.
